messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bao, a thirty-five-year-old accountant, presents as a man holding himself together with immense effort. The trauma occurred just over a year ago, during what was meant to be a routine business trip. He was in a foreign city, mistaken for someone else by a group of men. What began with unsettlingly polite questions in a back room escalated over several hours into a period of interrogation and torture he struggles to coherently describe. He was eventually released, left on a street corner with the chilling realization that his captors had simply gotten the wrong person. Since returning home, the structure of his life has systematically dismantled.

The memories of the event do not feel like his own. When he speaks about it, it is with a strange detachment, as if he is narrating a film he was forced to watch. He had come to believe this was a mercy, this sense of the memory being alien, but the film plays on a loop regardless. A specific scene—the glint of a tool on a metal table, the sound of laughter—replays without warning, often triggered by nothing he can identify. When he tries to consciously piece together what happened, the sequence dissolves. He knows he was taken from the street, and he remembers being let go, but the hours in between are a confusing jumble of sensory fragments, making it impossible to construct a linear narrative of the ordeal. This confusion fuels a deep-seated shame; he feels that somebody else, someone stronger or quicker-witted, would have been able to stop what was happening, or at least make sense of it afterward.

This sense of a fractured self and a dangerous world now governs his daily existence. At his accounting firm, a place once defined by predictable order, he is paralyzed by the simplest of professional interactions. When a potential new client is introduced, Bao’s focus dissolves. The stranger’s outstretched hand, their friendly questions about his services, are perceived not as professional courtesy but as a prelude to an unknown threat. He has come to believe with absolute certainty that you can never know who will harm you. This conviction has led him to refuse all new client intakes, a decision that has strained his relationship with his partners and stalled his career. He now works exclusively with long-standing accounts, his professional world shrinking to a small, manageable list of familiar names.

His personal life has suffered even more acutely. His ex-wife, he explains, tried for months to be patient. But any conversation about their life together—planning a vacation, discussing a mortgage, even deciding what to do next weekend—became a minefield. The concept of the future, once a source of shared excitement, now felt to Bao like an unbearable provocation. His captors had taunted him about the things they were going to do, mocking any future he thought he had. Now, any talk of plans brings on a wave of visceral dread, and he would shut down, unable to participate. The cumulative effect of this withdrawal led to their separation six months ago, a development that confirmed his most profound fear: that the experience did not just happen *to* him, but that it has permanently changed him for the worse. He feels he is no longer the man his wife married, but a damaged, lesser version.

Bao sought therapy after receiving a formal warning at work regarding his refusal to engage with new business. The threat of losing the last stable pillar of his life—his job—was the final impetus. He sits in the therapy room, a portrait of quiet desperation, terrified that his belief is true and he is broken beyond repair. His stated goal for therapy is not happiness, but simply to be able to have a conversation with a stranger without feeling like his life is in danger, a modest hope that feels, to him, impossibly ambitious.
